n0001.title: Towards a Theory of Bugs
n0001.gist: Bugs are unavoidable in any program that does real work, because simple programs can behave in ways nobody can foresee.
n0001.question: Theory of bugs — why can't bugs be fully eliminated from useful programs? (an argument with examples)
n0001.sourceHeading: Towards a Theory of Bugs: The Ruliology of the Unexpected

n0002.title: “My Program Did the Wrong Thing!”
n0002.gist: Bugs can be studied scientifically, since even tiny programs show them, and the unforeseeable behavior of simple programs explains why they arise.
n0002.question: Bugs — why can even very simple programs surprise us? (an outline of the argument)

n0003.title: Can bugs have a theory
n0003.gist: Bugs are everywhere and each seems unique, yet the essay asks whether a general scientific theory of them is possible, built on unpredictability in computation.

n0011.title: Simple programs, unforeseen behavior
n0011.gist: A program is meant to follow a simple picture in our heads, but even simple programs can compute in ways we cannot foresee, and we call those surprises bugs.

n0015.title: Bugs in Turing Machines
n0015.gist: Tiny Turing machines that seem to add 1 to a number fail at surprisingly large inputs, such as 7 or 63.
n0015.question: Turing machines — how far must one test before a hidden bug shows up? (worked examples)

n0016.title: A machine that fails at 7
n0016.gist: A 3-state machine seems to compute n + 1 but outputs 9 for input 7, with glitches at every number of the form 8k – 1.

n0029.title: Correct machines and late bugs
n0029.gist: Many machines correctly compute n + 1, but some only fail at n = 15 or n = 63, and the riskiest inputs are those written in binary as all 1s.

n0050.title: What Counts as a Bug?
n0050.gist: A bug exists only relative to a specification other than the program itself, and for every kind of specification some machines obey it until suddenly failing.
n0050.question: Specifications — what makes a program's behavior count as a bug? (several kinds of specification)

n0051.title: Specifications beyond the program
n0051.gist: A program always does what it does, so bugs only exist against an easier-to-grasp specification, such as a restatement in another language or another program.

n0061.title: Prohibitions and output constraints
n0061.gist: Specifications can forbid behaviors like unbounded tape use, infinite loops or odd outputs, yet some machines appear to obey until a late input, like n = 42, 151 or 32.

n0077.title: A Cellular Automaton Example
n0077.gist: Cellular automata built to double their input show the same pattern: many work, but some fail only after a long wait.
n0077.question: Cellular automata — do bugs appear there as they do in Turing machines? (examples)

n0091.title: Can One Tell If There’s Going to Be a Bug?
n0091.gist: Visual simplicity can rule out bugs, but complicated cases cannot be settled by testing or fluctuation statistics, though a structural argument sometimes proves no bug ever occurs.
n0091.question: Bug prediction — how can we tell in advance whether a bug will occur? (cases and an argument)
n0091.sourceHeading: Can One Tell If There’s Going to Be a Bug?

n0092.title: Simple versus puzzling patterns
n0092.gist: Some patterns obviously double correctly, but others look like known buggy ones, and the stabilization time fits a trend with random-looking fluctuations that nothing can bound.

n0112.title: Proving a complicated case safe
n0112.gist: Looking at the whole computation shows a left-moving boundary and an inner rule 122 pattern that can never die out, so this complicated automaton never fails.

n0127.title: But What about Formal Proofs?
n0127.gist: Formal proofs can show some machines never fail, but a proof is no cheaper than running the machine, and no proof exists for a buggy one.
n0127.question: Formal proofs — can they guarantee a program has no bugs, and at what cost? (a worked proof)

n0128.title: Setting up the proof
n0128.gist: Writing the tape and rules as symbolic expressions turns the claim that the machine computes n + 1 for all inputs into a statement an automated prover can handle.

n0157.title: The proof and its limits
n0157.gist: An automated proof using induction covers all inputs for simple machines, but proofs grow long for harder ones, and none can exist for buggy machines.

n0174.title: Proof versus running the machine
n0174.gist: Searching for a proof costs as much unbounded effort as testing cases, whether done through equational logic or the type-theory approach used by proof assistants.

n0178.title: Computational Irreducibility and Bugs
n0178.gist: Bugs ultimately come from computational irreducibility, where behavior can only be found by running the program, and that is also what makes computation worth doing.
n0178.question: Computational irreducibility — why can't bugs be ruled out in advance? (a general argument)

n0189.title: Did I Test Enough Cases? The Failure of Ruliological Induction
n0189.gist: Testing many cases and assuming the pattern holds fails in the study of simple programs, because bugs can be arbitrarily rare and show up only after huge numbers of samples.
n0189.question: Induction — why does testing many cases fail to show a program is bug-free? (an argument)
n0189.sourceHeading: Did I Test Enough Cases? The Failure of Ruliological Induction

n0201.title: Some Typical Ruliological Surprises
n0201.gist: Across rules, machines, initial conditions and other systems, surprising behavior appears often and late, so bugs are the rule rather than the exception in this field.
n0201.question: Ruliological surprises — how common are unexpected behaviors in simple systems? (a series of examples)

n0233.title: Mathematical “Bugs”
n0233.gist: Mathematics has counterexamples like x105 – 1 and a prime-count flip, but pure mathematics mostly stays in human-level pockets of predictability, though experimental mathematics is exposed like ruliology.
n0233.question: Mathematics — why does it run into bugs less often than ruliology? (examples and an explanation)

n0248.title: Bugs in Practice
n0248.gist: Bugs cannot be eliminated from useful programs, but good language design, seeing inside the computation, and tolerating some approximation help, and bugs count as discoveries in science.
n0248.question: Practical bug handling — what can we do when bugs cannot be eliminated? (a set of strategies)
